reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by Pasteurella multocida, a Gram-negative coccobacillus that is a common commensal in the mouths of cats and dogs, and usually acquired through animal bites or scratches, particularly from cats
Soft-tissue infection develops strikingly rapidly, often within hours of a cat bite, with intense pain, erythema, swelling and a serosanguinous or purulent discharge
The speed of onset helps distinguish it from staphylococcal and streptococcal wound infections, which typically evolve more slowly
Deep hand bites are prone to spread to tendon sheaths, joints and bone, causing tenosynovitis, septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, so hand wounds warrant careful assessment
Non-bite disease, including respiratory infection and, in vulnerable hosts, bacteraemia and meningitis, can follow close animal contact without an obvious wound

Co-amoxiclav is a standard choice because it covers Pasteurella together with the other mouth flora and skin organisms in bite wounds; notably many oral agents such as flucloxacillin and first-generation cephalosporins have poor activity against Pasteurella
Wound management, thorough irrigation, consideration of leaving bite wounds open, and assessment of tetanus and rabies risk are integral to care
reference.pathophysiology: Pasteurella multocida is inoculated into tissue when an animal bites or scratches, or when saliva contaminates an existing wound. The organism produces virulence factors, including a polysaccharide capsule and endotoxin, that provoke a brisk acute inflammatory response, accounting for the characteristically rapid onset of pain, erythema and swelling. Because bites deposit organisms deep in tissue, infection can track along tendon sheaths and reach joints and bone, and in hosts with impaired defences, chronic liver disease or immunosuppression the organism may invade the bloodstream and seed distant sites such as the meninges, respiratory tract and prosthetic material.
additionalDifferentials: Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection after a dog bite
additionalInvestigations: Culture of wound exudate or aspirated pus, informing the laboratory of the animal-bite context
Blood cultures where systemic infection is suspected
Gram stain of exudate showing Gram-negative coccobacilli
Plain radiography of the affected part to detect osteomyelitis or a retained foreign body such as a tooth fragment
Cross-sectional imaging or surgical exploration for suspected deep-space hand infection
redFlags: Deep hand or joint involvement with signs of tenosynovitis or septic arthritis
Rapidly spreading infection or features suggesting a necrotising process
Meningitis or respiratory infection in a vulnerable host
Underlying immunosuppression, asplenia or chronic liver disease predisposing to invasive disease
reference.prognosis: Most localised bite-associated Pasteurella infections resolve well with appropriate antibiotics and wound care, but deep hand infections can cause lasting functional impairment, and invasive disease such as bacteraemia or meningitis carries significant mortality, particularly in comorbid patients.
pitfalls: Choosing an antibiotic such as flucloxacillin or a first-generation cephalosporin with poor Pasteurella activity for a bite wound
Underestimating a small cat-bite puncture that has inoculated organisms deep into tissue
Missing early tenosynovitis or joint involvement in hand bites
Neglecting tetanus and rabies risk assessment
Assuming systemic disease cannot occur without an obvious bite wound
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Start empirical co-amoxiclav, which covers Pasteurella multocida together with other mouth and skin flora in bite wounds, avoiding flucloxacillin and first-generation cephalosporins that lack reliable Pasteurella activity
Use doxycycline, a fluoroquinolone, or a macrolide as alternatives in penicillin-allergic patients
Provide thorough wound irrigation and debridement, leaving bite wounds open rather than tightly closed
Undertake surgical drainage or washout for deep-space hand infection, tenosynovitis, or septic arthritis
Treat invasive disease such as bacteraemia or meningitis with an intravenous beta-lactam such as benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone
Give tetanus prophylaxis and assess rabies risk according to the animal and exposure
Arrange radiography for suspected osteomyelitis, refer deep hand infections to a hand surgeon, and account for host vulnerability such as immunosuppression or chronic liver disease
